lesson.title: The Payoff Molecule: From G3P to Glucose
lesson.summary: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate is the actual usable product exiting the Calvin cycle, and plants convert it into glucose, sucrose, starch, and the raw material for nearly every other organic molecule they build.
lesson.body:
After carbon dioxide is fixed by RuBisCO and the resulting three-carbon compound is reduced using ATP and NADPH, the molecule that comes out the other side is glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate, universally abbreviated G3P. This is the actual chemical payoff of the entire Calvin cycle, the point where energy that started as sunlight, passed through an electron transport chain, crossed a membrane as a proton gradient, and got captured by ATP synthase, finally ends up stored in a stable carbon-hydrogen bond that a cell can keep around indefinitely rather than spending within seconds.

Most of the G3P a chloroplast produces never leaves the Calvin cycle at all, since the cycle needs to spend five out of every six G3P molecules just to regenerate the ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate that carbon fixation consumes. It takes three turns of the cycle, three carbon dioxide molecules fixed by RuBisCO, to yield a single net G3P molecule available for anything else, and two of those net G3P molecules, representing six fixed carbons in total, are what a plant combines to build one molecule of glucose.

Converting two G3P molecules into a glucose molecule involves a set of reactions that runs largely in reverse of early glycolysis, the pathway cells use to break glucose down, which is a useful thing to notice: G3P is not just a Calvin cycle product, it is also a genuine glycolytic intermediate, meaning the same three-carbon molecule sits at a crossroads between building sugar and breaking sugar down, depending on which direction the surrounding chemistry pushes it.

Glucose itself is often just an intermediate destination rather than a final one. Plants commonly link two sugar units together to form sucrose, a transportable form that gets exported out of the leaf through the plant's vascular tissue to feed roots, developing fruit, and other tissues that cannot photosynthesize for themselves. Alternatively, glucose units can be strung together into long branching chains to form starch, which gets stored inside the chloroplast itself as a temporary energy reserve, ready to be broken back down at night when the light reactions are not running. Carbon skeletons derived from G3P and its downstream sugars also feed into the synthesis of amino acids, fatty acids, and the cellulose that builds plant cell walls, so the reach of this single molecule extends across nearly the entire chemistry of the plant.

Seen this way, G3P production is the real finish line of photosynthesis. The light-dependent reactions and the carbon-fixing machinery of RuBisCO exist, from the plant's perspective, to deliver a steady stream of this one three-carbon molecule, and everything downstream, from the sugar in a grain of wheat to the wood in a tree trunk, traces back to carbon atoms that passed through G3P on their way out of the Calvin cycle.
